speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like
to make an announcement regarding trade conferences. Last week, as hon. members know, a meeting of the Canada-United Kingdom continuing committee was held here in Ottawa, and during the week end my colleague, the minister of external affairs (Mr. Pearson), issued a short summary of the profitable discussions which took place. Discussions with the British West Indies followed the United Kingdom talks and are now completed.
A delegation of officials of the French government arrived in Ottawa this morning to discuss a number of problems pertaining to trade between our two countries. Members of this delegation spent yesterday in Toronto at the international trade fair, where they were welcomed as honoured guests and were able to see the merchandise of many countries now on display there. This afternoon the French delegation will begin meetings with officials of government departments concerned. It is expected that these discussions will be carried on for two or three days. The tariff agreement completed recently at Torquay between Canada and France was evidence of the desire which exists on both sides to create opportunities for trade.
Tomorrow, May 30, the minister of customs of New Zealand, who is also the associate minister of finance of that country, will arrive in Ottawa to discuss trade problems with the Canadian government. We welcome this timely visit of a distinguished minister of the crown from a sister commonwealth country. Canada has traditionally enjoyed
valuable trade relations with New Zealand, and we hope that the groundwork will be laid at the present meetings for further expansion.

RULES RESPECTING STRANGERS IN THE GALLERY AND SUBJECTS OF QUESTIONS OF PRIVILEGE- ASKING OF QUESTIONS-READING OF SPEECHES
speechtext:
May I be permitted to make a statement at this time. A few days ago the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) brought to my attention a practice which is becoming very common in the house of hon. members rising on so-called questions of privilege. This irregularity has also been brought to my attention by other hon. members from time to time throughout the session, and more especially during recent weeks. It has also been the subject of unfavourable comment in the press.
There are only two types of questions of privilege. One affects a member personally and is a matter of personal privilege, and the other is one which affects the privileges of all hon. members of the house. It is neither a question of personal privilege nor one which affects the privileges of all hon. members to inform the house that an athletic organization or any organization, or any citizen or citizens, have brought distinction to a member's constituency by winning a championship. Nor is it a question of privilege to bring to the attention of the house the fact that certain school children or others are in the gallery. No reference should1 at any time be made to the gallery except on the occasion of the attendance in the gallery of a distinguished representative of another country. It is highly improper at any other time to refer to the gallery. If the practice continues, either of referring to championship teams or to school children in the gallery, every hon. member will feel called upon to do likewise when occasion arises, as otherwise he will feel that his constituents may think
fMr. Howe.]
that he is ignoring them. May I therefore suggest to hon. members that they refrain in the future from making these references.
There is another matter to which I think reference should be made at this time. It is with respect to the procedure regarding the asking of questions. I would refer hon. members to standing order No. 44. This standing order provides for the placing of questions on the order paper, which is the usual procedure, and should be followed whenever possible.
It has nevertheless been the practice in our house to allow a certain number of oral questions, and it is not my purpose to discourage members from asking questions of the proper type, as I feel that these questions create a more lively interest in the business of the house. These oral questions are asked when the orders of the day are called, and are frequently asked without notice. I would, however, emphasize that these oral questions should be asked only in connection with very urgent and important matters-of public concern, and only if it would not be in the public interest, to place them on the order paper and receive answers in accordance with the method provided for in the standing orders. They should always be brief. No debate is permitted, and the reply should be as concise as possible. The questions should not be prefaced by the reading of letters, telegrams, newspaper extracts or preambles of any kind. See Beauchesne's third edition, paragraphs 297, 298. I ask the co-operation of hon. members in observing these rules.
While I am making these references, may I also take the opportunity of thanking hon. members for the co-operation* which they have given; me in* my endeavour to enforce the rule which prohibits the reading by private members of previously prepared speeches. On February 20 of this year I reminded hon. members of the rule, and for a short time it was generally observed. However, during the debate on the budget a very considerable number of members reverted to the undesirable practice of reading their speeches. The reading of long speeches, especially by private members, would not be tolerated at Westminster, and I might point out that we would be required to follow the usages and customs of the British house if our standing orders did not prohibit the reading of speeches. The House of Commons is not a debating society nor an assembly which is gathered together to listen to the reading of essays. It is a forum where members may express themselves freely in accordance with the established rules on all matters of public interest.

I believe that during this session fewer speeches have been read than in former sessions, but I am very hopeful that the practice of reading speeches, except in the case of government statements or important statements by the leader of the opposition or by leaders of other groups, will be wholly discontinued.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, May 28, consideration in committee of Bill No. 192, to amend the Petition of Right Act-Mr. Garson-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Filing of petition.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext:
Last evening the
minister spoke of the subject being placed in a position of equality with the crown. Any action the individual may desire to take against the crown must be taken in the exchequer court. The crown, however, may take proceedings in any court of competent jurisdiction of any province. When the crown chooses to take proceedings in a court set up within a province-the court of king's bench, the supreme court, trial division, or the county court-the subject may raise matters in defence as against the crown but is denied the right to counter-claim. That places the subject in an impossible position,

and I suggest for the consideration of the minister that a change is due in that respect. Where the crown chooses to accept the jurisdiction of a court other than the exchequer court and commences its action there, the citizen should not be placed in such a position that a counter-claim may not be presented in that court. This is a matter which might well be considered by the law officers of the crown.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend quoted my remarks accurately, so perhaps for the record I had better repeat what I said as reported at page 3479 of Hansard:
The purpose of this legislation is to place the crown in right of Canada in petition of right proceedings in the exchequer court in substantially the same position as an ordinary litigant.
That is what this bill does. My hon. friend raises a question which I think he will admit is quite different from that which is involved in this bill, namely, that in those infrequent cases in which the crown chooses another court in which to sue the subject, consideration should be given to enabling the litigant against whom such suit is taken in that other court to raise such defences or offsets as are available to him in the exchequer court. I have no hesitation in saying that we should be very glad to give my hon. friend's suggestion due consideration, but it is hardly relevant to the bill before the committee.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext: On the narrow ground of relevancy to the matter in issue here, I am not in disagreement with the minister. But when so much ado is made about the position of a citizen in his relation in litigation-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext: In the exchequer court.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext:
-in the exchequer court, yes; but most laymen would not get the distinction that lawyers would make in the use of the words "the exchequer court". I know of one or more cases in which the defendant has been unable properly to defend himself in the court chosen as the forum by the crown, by reason of the fact he was unable to make a counter-claim.
Let me refer again to the matter I mentioned last evening. Under this legislation, parliament is actually divesting the crown of one of its most ancient prerogatives without having secured the consent of the crown to the legislation. I mentioned that because, after all, the king is one of the three component parts of parliament. The king, it is true, acts upon the advice of his privy council; nevertheless there are certain cases in which the king is freed from acting on the advice of his council.
80709-223i
Petition of Right Act
My reading of the constitutional development of kingship indicates that this prerogative is not a mere fiction or formality, but rather one of the most prized positions that kingship holds, not only by virtue of tradition, but also by reason of the fact that the king occupies so important a position in the constitutional development of the country. Last evening the member for Rosetown-Biggar said that, after all, we have not a king in Canada. That is scarcely in accordance with the constitutional development about which I have heard boasting in this house in recent years, particularly since the Statute of Westminster. To those who say that the king occupies an unimportant position and is merely a symbol, the answer is that so long as there is a king there can be no dictatorship within the British commonwealth. The king is above politics; he chooses his advisers following the decision made by the electors; in fact, he determines who shall be his prime minister and his first citizen.
That kingship is no mere symbol, and that the king has tremendous influence was indicated in England in 1922 or 1923, when everyone in the Conservative party believed that the king would call Earl Curzon to be prime minister, but the king chose to call Mr. Baldwin to that office. I repeat that the office of kingship is no mere formality. It is a symbol which binds us together. But in addition under our constitutional development, the kingship denies the possibility of there ever being a dictatorship so long as that kingship exists, and so long as the king carries out that responsibility which rests with him and no one else. Therefore I ask that nothing be done by this parliament which would in any way appear to detract or subtract from one of the prerogatives of kingship, namely, that the king can do no wrong. This principle antedates cabinet responsibility and all that cabinet responsibility means. The significance of it is that the king is above the law by reason of his prerogative right of not being subject to the king's courts.
The minister has had the opinion of the law officers of the crown, and I have done my duty. But certainly one can take Hansard after Hansard back to 1835, and wherever there has been any removal or subtraction of the right of kingship-indeed, even a change of title to be given to His Majesty-the announcement was made by the king's minister that His Majesty was willing to accept whatever decision was made by parliament. Even when Edward VIII abdicated in 1936 that formula was used, and he in fact con- 1 sented, as the constitutional monarch, to the ]

I	Petition of Right Act
removal from him of all his prerogatives before parliament accepted his abdication.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext:
It is both interesting and refreshing, Mr. Chairman, to hear the Minister of Justice this afternoon drawing attention to certain limitations of the bill now before the committee. Last evening, if one is to judge from his remarks in certain places, one would have thought that in its effect this was a broad and sweeping measure. As is shown by the report of the proceedings in the committee, at page 3489 of Hansard, the minister complained that the hon. member for Lake Centre had put a rather narrow interpretation on the effect of the measure. At the bottom of the page the minister is reported as follows:
While I am on that subject, I believe that, in fairness to our own legislation, I should point out that the hon. member for Lake Centre rather 
tended to leave the impression that the scope of our act was quite narrow. I believe I should point out what it does cover.
Then the minister went on to deal with some of the sections of the Exchequer Court Act, a statute which has such a direct bearing on the subject now under discussion. But this afternoon the minister has done a service in assisting the committee to realize that the measure, after all, is somewhat narrow in its terms and in its effect. He has drawn attention to certain narrowing words that he used in introducing the measure, as reported at page 3479 of Hansard, when he said:
The purpose of this legislation is to place the crown in right of Canada in petition of right proceedings in the exchequer court in substantially the same position as an ordinary litigant.
It is highly commendable that the minister this afternoon should have placed such great emphasis on those words "in petition of right proceedings in the exchequer court," because otherwise the effect of the statement made by the minister last night, it seems to me, was to exaggerate considerably the effect of the present measure. The minister has now helped the committee to see the bill in its proper perspective which, after all, is quite a narrow one.
In effect, this measure deals with a procedural question and eliminates a step in procedure. It does not affect the substantive law. If the principle upon which the government is proceeding is sound, and I believe it is, we should have had with this measure corresponding amendments to the substantive law of Canada, so that what we are doing here, in deference to a principle, should have real substance and not be simply a change in what is, after all, little more than procedure and form. While commending the present measure as far as it goes-and I regret that it does not go very far-I wish to record my regret that the government has not gone as far as it might well have gone, and ought to have gone, in view of the soundness of the principle supporting this type of legislation.
I could not help recalling a debate that occurred in the house on December 13, 1945. At that time the present Prime Minister was minister of justice, and I asked him this question on his estimates, as reported at page 3467 of Hansard of that session:
What progress, if any, is being made in the department with reference to the matter of petitions of right? It has been such a sore point for so long, and I think the courts and the bar are looking for some leadership in this matter. I know the Minister of Justice has had this matter brought actively before him for a long time. When may we look for some action in the direction of elimination of petitions of right in actions against the crown?

And the answer came back, very swift and very firm:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext:
Not while I am Minister of
Justice.
It is evident that since the present Prime Minister ceased to be minister of justice there has been a change of heart on his part; and I think the committee will be glad to see such a change of heart on the part of the government, because the position taken by the then minister of justice, the present Prime Minister, is, I think, a position which the government, in introducing the present measure, has shown to have been entirely unsound. I am glad the government has made sufficient progress at least to have discarded the position taken in 1945 by the Prime Minister and to have introduced the present measure, limited though its effect may be.
A good deal has been said in this discussion about the historical background of the immunities of the crown, and about the way in which the procedure for petition of right has grown up and has been observed for centuries. An interesting description of those immunities was given by Chief Justice Duff in the case of the King v. Central Railway Signal Company, 1933 Supreme Court Reports, where, at page 564, after reviewing the immunities enjoyed by the crown in respect of torts and certain other forms of action, the chief justice says this:
It has sometimes been said that this immunity of the sovereign from processual coercion, "the grandest of his immunities," to use the words of Maitland . . . rests upon the principle that the king by his writ cannot command himself, and this was laid down in the Sadler's case; the immunity has also been ascribed to the fact that the courts are the king's own courts and to the same principle as that of the immunity of the feudal seigneur from process in his seigneurial court.
What the government is proposing in this measure is that there should be a measure designed to strip the crown of some of the procedural or formal aspects of what has here been called the crown's "immunity from processual coercion", "the grandest of the immunities of the crown". If the principle of this bill is sound, it is sound enough to be extended to the substantive law, where it should be given full recognition. It is not given full recognition today.
In his remarks last night the Minister of Justice dwelt at some length on some of the subsections of section 19 of the Exchequer Court Act; but I think the Minister of Justice will agree that there are still great areas of what would be liability in the case of an ordinary litigant, in which fields the crown is still immune, regardless of however tortious the acts of the crown or the crown's servants
Petition of Right Act
might have been, if those acts had been committed by a private litigant or by servants or employees of a private litigant.
There is much to be said in this day and generation for a discarding of this type of immunity of the crown. We recognized the same principle last year in the Statute Law Amendment Act, when so many emanations of the crown in the form of statutory corporations were brought, by enactment of parliament, under liability to action in the courts for breach of law. That was a sound type of legislation. It is a recognition not simply of the soundness of a principle but also of the fact that, as the power of government grows, expands, and is wielded, more and more of the area of what years ago had been regarded as fields closed to government and belonging exclusively to fields of operation on the part of private citizens is now enclosed within the scope of governmental operations. Therefore, old principles and old immunities which had a sound bearing in days when the activities of the crown, so far as the ordinary business of life was concerned, were on a very narrow scale indeed, do not fit the situation that obtains today, when governments are operating in so many fields of what were previously exclusively private endeavour. Last year's amendment was sound; this amendment is sound, but I still say that it does not go far enough in bringing about justice and fair play to litigants.
The hon. member for Lake Centre referred this afternoon to a situation where, in an action brought by the crown against a private litigant, the litigant is not free to make a counter-claim in the proceedings. That smacks of injustice and a lack of a sense of fair play in days such as these. I do not believe that the people of Canada have any patience in these days with immunities of the crown which have no sensible bearing upon the hard facts of governmental operations.
The Canadian Bar Association has1 for years been pressing the government on this subject.
Sir, there are good precedents for widening such provisions as we find in the present section of the bill under discussion. Some of the provinces have taken wholesome steps in this regard. You will find them in, P.C. 43/1880 of May 14, 1947, amended by P.C. 254J/2727 of May 28, 1949. This first -order in -council -contains this as the third clause:

And clause 2-D of the order defines officer or servant of the crown as follows:

Then follow the detailed' provisions governing -procedure in claims arising under clause 3.
It seems to me that the time has come when there should be an effective consolidation, with the necessary broadening of the provisions, of our law, whether statutory or in order in council -form, as in the case of these two orders in council, and others I believe as well, to meet the needs of the present day, and also to give effective codification to the

I expect some hon. members have had experience with these orders in council that were in effect during the war, and with perhaps the two to which I have just referred, which came into effect after the war. I think the experience of any who have had cases under these orders in council has been unsatisfactory. They must have come to the conclusion that these are entirely unsatisfactory provisions for the statement of the liability of the crown for acts of the officers or members of the armed forces of Canada or employees of the Department of National Defence.
I remember a case that occurred in connection with naval gunnery practice in lake Ontario, close to fishing claims very near to Toronto, where great damage was done to the fishing as well as to the nets and other property of the licensee of those fishing claims. The affidavits of about eight eye-witnesses of the shelling and the consequent damage to fishing and fish nets and equipment were submitted: to the Department of National Defence in due course. I regret to say that the matter received pretty summary treatment in the Department of National Defence, and the claim was not entertained.
There is only one way in which private claimants will at best feel that they have had a fair hearing of a case or that justice has been done, and that is if they are allowed to take their cases to the courts for adjudication. If the judicial processes offered by the crown to govern disputes between private litigants are good enough for them, they ought equally to be good enough for the government which is largely responsible for prescribing those judicial processes for the settlement of the claims of others. Our conception of the rule of law should not be impaired or restricted by any narrow limitations which trace themselves back to regal immunities which simply do not fit the hard facts of times such as these, when governmental activities cover so many fields.
I urge upon the minister the broadening of the substantive law by statute, and I urge upon him also that he take orders in council of this kind under review to see to it that the government, having made a sound departure from the untenable and unsound position taken by the present Prime Minister in December, 1945, go further and, rather than contenting itself with half measures or a half-hearted recognition of a sound principle, bring in a measure that will give full and complete recognition to the desirability of extending the judicial process in the broadest possible sense to the settlement of just claims brought against the crown.

It goes back to the thirteenth century, and was intended to protect the citizen against the government.
There is a great deal of loose thinking in connection with constitutional matters, and people easily confuse the government with the king. The fact is that the king is a separate branch of government. To begin with, I have nothing to add to what I said yesterday to the effect that, in so far as section 19 (c) of the Exchequer Court Act and the liability thereunder is concerned, the crown is only liable in tort if negligence by an officer or servant of the crown acting within the scope of his duties or employment is first established. The case to which my hon. friend referred as being covered by the clipping which he sent to me bears that out. That was the case of Dame Elizabeth Cornell Oakes v. His Majesty the King. The first paragraph of the judgment of Mr. Justice Cameron of the exchequer court refers to the point of negligence in these terms:
This is a petition of right in which the suppliant claims damages from the respondent. On June 5, 1945, George Walsh Oakes, then an airman in the Royal Canadian Air Force, was a passenger in a motor vehicle owned by the respondent: that vehicle was struck by a train of the Canadian National Railways in Montreal east, and Oakes was killed. At the trial it was admitted that L.A.C. Oakes was then on duty, that the motor vehicle was operated by L.A.C. R. E. Hitsman, a member of the air force of Canada and then acting within the scope of his military duties, and that the said accident occurred because of the fault and negligence of the said Hitsman.
Therefore nothing turns, in the point raised by my hon. friend's question, upon whether there was negligence. In fact there was negligence in that case. My hon. friend's question must turn on another point and if I understand correctly the point that my hon. friend is driving at, I think perhaps I- can answer his question in these terms. I will go back a bit in order to cover the preliminary ground. In Meloche v. The King (1948) 4 D.L.R., 828, Mr. Justice Anger of the exchequer court held that a petition of right will not lie under section 19 (c) of the Exchequer Court Act for death or injury to
Petition of Right Act
a member of the forces in the course of his employment on the ground that parliament had by the Pension Act provided a special remedy for such death or injury; that is even where there may be negligence, and which otherwise would make the crown actionable.
In Bender v. The King (1947) S.C.R. 172, the Supreme Court of Canada held that a government employee who had received compensation under the Government Employees Compensation Act was nevertheless entitled to claim damages under said section 19 (c). Perhaps I should explain that the Government Employees Compensation Act is an act passed by this parliament to provide for federal civil servants a protection analogous to that which is enjoyed by workmen under the workmen's compensation acts of the various provinces. The Government Employees Compensation Act is another reason why comparisons between the liability of the crown under the Canadian Exchequer Court Act and under analogous British legislation are rather invidious because here is a whole field of torts arising out of the relationship of master and servant which is pretty well completely covered by the Government Employees Compensation Act in this country.
After the judgment in Bender v. The King, the Government Employees Compensation Act was revised by chapter 18 of the statutes of 1947, and section 9, subsection 5, thereof now reads as follows:
No employee or dependent of such employee shall have a claim against His Majesty or any officer, servant or agent of His Majesty, except for compensation under this act, in any case where an accident happens to such employee in the course of his employment under such circumstances as entitle him or his dependents to compensation under this act.
That is simply the principle followed in workmen's compensation acts, that once workmen's compensation acts are put on the statute books all claims based upon negligence as between master and servant, and as between one employee and another employee, are washed out, and the provision made by that act in the form of workmen's compensation insurance takes their place. Coming down to the case of Oakes v. The King to which my hon. friend has referred, Mr. Justice Cameron of the Exchequer Court of Canada, on May 17 last, handed down his decision in that case holding that he was bound by the reasoning of the supreme court in the Bender case to overrule the judgment of Mr. Justice Anger in the Meloche case. Therefore, by that process of reasoning, he awarded Mrs. Oakes, the wife of the airman killed in the course of duty as a result of

Petition of Right Act
admitted negligence, the sum of $20,000 in addition to any rights she might have in regard to pension and the like.
That is the situation as it stands today. If I understand my hon. friend's point- though I have not been too clear about it up to the present-it is that we should consider whether section 19 (c) does not go too far in the light of this judgment in the Oakes case, in that it will be imposing quite a burden on the taxpayer if, in addition to all the benefits under the Pension Act et cetera that may be available to the dependents of any member of the armed forces in the event of his death while on duty, it should be possible as well to enter suit against the crown and recover substantial damages, as for example the amount of $20,000 in this case. Is that not my hon. friend's point?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ABOLITION OF GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext:
I noted a few moments ago that the minister said it was his intention before third reading to indicate either the royal or vice regal consent to this legislation. I have no serious objection to the minister doing that, particularly when he puts it on the basis he does, namely out of the abundance of caution; but I should like to take a moment or two to express my own view that this course is quite unnecessary and I think it is unfair both to the houses of parliament and the crown.
With regard to my first point I suggest that in our legislative functions we are governed by the British North America Act, which contains only two qualifications with respect to the way in which we pass bills. Those two qualifications are found in sections 53 and 54. Section 53 provides that money bills must originate in the House of Commons. Section 54 is the section which says that before any money bill is proceeded with the approval of the governor general must be stated in parliament. The only reason royal consent or approval to some bills is indicated is that with respect to those particular bills, that is money bills, it is actually required by the British North America Act. Frankly, if it were not in that act I should think the practice might be reconsidered for a reason I shall indicate in a moment. But why should we go beyond what is required by the British North America Act and bring in a formula with respect to a bill which is not required either by the British North America Act or by the standing orders of this house?
The other point I wish to make is that I regard it as unfair, both to the houses of parliament and to the crown, to follow the proposed procedure. After all it is in parliament, in the Senate and House of Commons, that these decisions are really made. To carry forward the fiction that we make only such decisions as we are permitted by the crown to make is I think unfair to the two houses of parliament and out of keeping with the democratic practice under which we in parliament initiate and pass legislation. Similarly I think it is unfair to the crown. The Minister of Justice brought in this bill, moved first reading, moved second reading, and has piloted it through the committee stage. Obviously the government decided to go ahead with this bill. The House of Commons has accepted it; indeed we have approved of it right along. Now the minister says that just before third reading he is going to announce to parliament that the crown gives its approval to our considering this bill. Well, that would seem to mean that the minister has personally consulted either the king or the governor general and has requested that approval. Under our modern

set-up the crown will not refuse such a request; in other words the crown is told what to do, and I submit that we are going through forms just for the sake of keeping up forms which are not necessary and are a bit unfair to both parties. We keep up the form with regard to the introduction of money bills because it is spelled out in the British North America Act. But why go further? Why make such an announcement in connection with this bill, which is not a money bill? The British North America Act also requires that before any bill which has been passed by both houses of parliament becomes law, it must have the royal assent given in the name of the king. That will come later; surely that final royal assent is sufficient.
As I have said, I have no serious objection to the minister following the course he has indicated in response to the request that was made of him by the official opposition, but I still feel that it is quite unnecessary.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill provides for just three very minor amendments to the Quebec Savings Banks Act. This act applies to two small savings banks in the province of Quebec. One is the Montreal City and District Savings Bank, and the other is the Quebec Savings Bank. Both are old banks, one having been incorporated in 1846 and the other in 1848. They are not commercial banks in the ordinary sense of the word and do not come under the Bank Act. This Quebec Savings Banks Act applies quite severe restrictions on the investments and loans which these banks may make, such as no commercial loans, and personal loans being limited to $1,000. At least fifty per cent of the bank deposits must be in government bonds. The banks have been permitted to invest in the bonds or debentures of a manufacturing company, provided, among other things, there have been paid upon the common stock of the company regular dividends of at least four per cent per annum for the five years preceding the investment. In the case of no par value shares there must have been a dividend of at least four dollars per share per annum the five years preceding the investment. The banks are also permitted to lend money without collateral security to certain companies if, among other things, similar rates of dividends have been paid on the common or no par value stock.
The reason for this amendment is that, whereas in other days the common practice was for common stock to be worth around $100, and the four dollar dividend represented a rate of return of four per cent, there has been today a splitting of the stock down to values of $25 to make it more popular. The four dollar dividend demanded would, therefore, mean a higher rate of return. It is proposed to amend both of these provisions to require that the dividend rate upon the common shares in each year of the five-year period must be at least four per cent of the average value at which the shares were carried in the capital stock of the company during the year in which the dividend was paid. I might say that a similar amendment was made to the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act.
Under the act as it stands today these two savings banks are allowed to lend up to five per cent of their deposits on first mortgages. That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Veterans Insurance Act to extend the scope of the act and the period during which a contract of insurance may be entered into; to increase the amount payable at time of death and, in certain cases, to permit the estate of the insured to receive the full amount payable under the policy contract; to provide for the insertion in the policy contract of a war clause in certain cases; and generally to improve the administration of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AMOUNT PAYABLE AT DEATH, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AMOUNT PAYABLE AT DEATH, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any explanation which I shall make of this resolution at this stage necessarily will be quite brief. As hon. members know, the Veterans Insurance Act, which was passed in 1944 and came into force in 1945, authorized the minister to enter into a policy of insurance with world war II veterans, and certain other groups of persons were added by an amendment in 1948. The time during which this authority could be exercised was extended and certain other groups were included. It is proposed now to further extend the period of time during which an insurance contract may be entered into until December 31, 1954. It is also proposed to give a veteran the right to enter into a contract within ten years after his discharge, if that date should be later than December 31, 1954.


One other provision is to authorize the sum of $2,000 to be paid in the event of the death of the insured. Hon. members are probably aware of the fact that, under the act as it stands now, the sum of $1,000 can be paid at the time of death, and the balance of the policy is paid in the form of annuities over a period of five, ten, fifteen or twenty years. In some cases it has been found that this method created certain difficulties in the settlement of the estate and the payment of medical and funeral expenses. It was felt, therefore, that the sum of $2,000 should be substituted for that $1,000.
Another provision which we have in mind is that, if no beneficiary or contingent beneficiary survives the insured, the face value of the policy would be paid to the estate. Under the present act only the insurance money to the extent of the reserve falls into the estate in case the insured dies without beneficiary or contingent beneficiary. We are also clarifying some of the sections in the act. For instance we want to make it clear that in the case where an applicant dies before the contract has been accepted and entered into by the department following his application, and where the premium has been paid, the insurance will be paid, provided it is an application that would have been accepted had the applicant not died before the acceptance. The reason for this change is that all these contracts are processed at headquarters, and there possibly could be some delay during which the insured might die before his application had been examined and accepted.
We are also clarifying the section of the act referring to the waiver of premiums in the event the insured suffers total and permanent disability. Under the present act, when such is the case, premiums are waived. But in the actual administration of the act it has been found exceedingly difficult to define or to determine the question of permanence of a disability and the period during which it has existed. We are therefore intending to make this legislation more easy to administer by specifying in the act that any insured who has suffered total disability continuously for one year will be considered as being totally and permanently disabled for the purpose of the waiver of premiums.
There is also another provision which we wish to introduce, since the question has been raised at various times as to whether insurance contracts under this act come within certain provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act. I think hon. members will recall that the same question arose

with regard to the Veterans Land Act some years ago, and a special section was included in the act so that the veterans of world war II who otherwise qualify, even if they are members of the House of Commons or of the Senate, can benefit under this act.

MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 322, respecting the Canada Post Office.

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: Is it the intention of the minister to make a general statement on the motion for second reading?

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: This being a complete revision of the Canada Post Office Act, and seeing that all the questions will be discussed separately on the various sections in committee, I thought that it might be more appropriate if I made my statement in committee.

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: I propose to speak on the motion for second reading, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that it is desirable for the minister to make a statement at this time because I am going to suggest reasons why we should not proceed with second reading until there has been further consideration of this bill.

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: I am absolutely in the hands of the house. This being a complete revision of the act, and as each section would be discussed1 in committee-

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: In order that the minister will not misunderstand me, may I explain that I would not be objecting to that procedure were it not for the fact that I feel that there are .certain objections to second reading which I shall put forward.

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said when introducing this bill on first reading, its purpose is to bring the post office legislation up to date, to bring its provisions in line with present practices and conditions, to simplify and clarify sections where necessary, to eliminate redundant and unnecessary provisions and to improve the general style and arrangement by reducing the law to a systematic form.
Hon. members will notice that in the printed bill reference is made in the explanatory notes to the relative sections of the existing act, and I want to make it clear that, even where this reference is made, although the essence is the same, the wording may vary in some cases, as an attempt has been made to simplify and clarify the section. It is my intention to ask the Clerk of the House to put on the table a number of copies of the old act so that, although the old act is not reproduced in this present bill, hon. members will be able to follow one section after the other.
There are thirty-nine provisions in the existing act which have been deleted. These include provisions which are now covered by other statutes or which have become obsolete.

Post Office Act
They also include certain extraordinary powers now vested in the Postmaster General and which I think should not be there.
Few people realize that under section 7 (p) of the present act, acting with the approval of the governor in council, the Postmaster General is authorized to impose pecuniary penalties not exceeding $200 for any one offence against any postal regulation, whether the person offending is or is not an officer of the post office. I do not know how long it is since a postmaster general has used this power. I know that I have not. This section is, of course, deleted and the power vested1, as it should be, in the courts of justice.
It might be a shock to the population of Canada to be refused change when they go to buy stamps; but any postmaster refusing to make change would be following the provisions of section 33 of the present act which binds him not to give change and to accept only-and this is the wording of the act- "the exact amount of the postage payable which must be tendered to him in current coin". This has been deleted.
Under section 34 of the present act the governor in council may direct that:
At any port or class of ports vessels shall not be permitted by the officers of customs to enter or break bulk until all letters on board the same have been delivered at the post office, nor until the master has made declaration, in such form as is prescribed, that he has delivered all such letters accordingly.
This also has been done away with.

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: What is the section?

maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Section 34 of the present act, which forbids the master of a vessel to allow passengers or cargo out of his vessels until and unless he has made a declaration that he has personally delivered all letters to the post office.
Present section 38 authorizes any person to seize any letters conveyed, received, collected, sent or delivered in violation of the present act.
These are a few of the sections which have been eliminated. I do not wish to burden the house with an enumeration of all the sections that will disappear with the enactment of the present bill.	*
The new bill introduces nine new definitions, fifteen new or amended provisions, eight sections dealing with the post office savings bank, section 47 and following, which are the same as those contained in the present Savings Bank Act, which is repealed by section 78 of the present bill. Section 55 and following dealing with offences and penalties are not strictly speaking new. They

have been recodified and amended in accordance with the form adopted with regard to new or revised acts. Hon. members will notice that sections 55 to 66 inclusive deal with indictable offences and sections 67 to 72 inclusive deal with offences. Section 73 is the penalty section.
It is not my intention, nor would it be proper at this stage, to discuss in detail each of the new provisions, but I am sure it will be noted by the hon. members that a distinction has been made between the administrative powers of the Postmaster General, which have been consolidated under one heading, namely, section 5, and his general powers to make regulations which itemize the outstanding features in regard to which regulations are required, section 6.
In this connection, I would like to draw hon. members' attention to the Postmaster General's power to fix rates. Rates in regard *to letters and publications generally are fixed by statute, by parliament; rates in regard to printed matter, parcel post and fees for services by the Postmaster General by regulation.
As regards letters the Postmaster General under section 8 has an exclusive privilege or a monopoly and it is therefore desirable that there should be parliamentary control of the rates charged the public.
Newspapers and publications are in a special class. Ever since the Post Office Act was enacted in 1867, the charges on newspapers and periodicals have been in the nature of a subsidy rate because they are media for the dissemination of news of religious, scientific, agricultural or current topics. In some cases, certain newspapers are even handled and carried without postal charge. There is, of course, no monopoly of the post office with regard to the handling of newspapers and periodicals. Publishers are at liberty to use whatever means of transportation and handling they may decide upon. Although there is no monopoly, there is, nevertheless, an element of government policy involved and for that reason, in the proposed act, no change has been made in the practice hitherto followed of having the rates on newspapers and periodicals fixed by parliament.
The situation is entirely different in regard to printed matter and parcel post. Government policy is not involved. There is no monopoly on the part of the post office and it is in competition with other agencies. The rates fluctuate and a degree of flexibility is essential in order that they be readily adjustable to take care of varying conditions at all times.

Hon. members will have noticed that the present bill proposes increases in the rates charged on newspapers and periodicals. These increases have been distributed equitably over each class of publication in relation to the strain imposed by each one on the facilities of the post office and to the varying cost of handling each.
In view of the mounting cost of postal operations, the government, in order to meet expenses, has had to increase its postal revenues. Some time ago, on April 2, we effected, by regulation, increases on parcel post, printed matter and registration fees, which could be done by regulation. Today, we are asking parliament to approve a somewhat similar increase on periodicals.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on Hansard the cost to the Post Office Department of handling newspapers and periodicals, second-class matter. In the last fiscal year which ended March 31-and I might say that the figure for next year will be somewhat higher on account of increases that have been given in wages and transportation costs-the cost of handling newspapers and periodicals was $15,816,015. The revenue we got from newspapers and, periodicals was $3,995,963, leaving a deficit in this one division of the post office of close to $12 million.
Letter rates are not touched but we are providing for the assimilation of war tax to postage in order to conform with the current practice. There is an apparent discrepancy between the new section 10, as to rates, and the old section 21 which mentions only one cent for so-called "drop letters", but the section of the Excise Tax Act providing for the extra 2 cents is repealed by the new section 78 of the Post Office Act.
Dealing now with the "drop letter" rate within certain municipal boundaries, I have received many representations from interested parties from this side of the house as well as from the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), from the city council of Ottawa and other persons outside this house, and I believe the bill now before the house will give the Postmaster General the necessary authority to cure the situation by authorizing him to establish and alter the limits of postal areas within which delivery of a letter therein posted may be effected for 3 cents.
I cannot in advance bind myself to follow exclusively the municipal boundaries, as a strict adherence to this principle enunciated by the leader of the opposition would forbid me to deliver, at the reduced rate, in areas not within the municipal boundaries which now receive that privilege. I feel sure that the leader of the opposition would not wish
Post Office Act
me to so describe the Ottawa postal area so as to exclude, for instance, Rockcliffe, or surrounding municipalities which now receive the drop-letter rate.
Last year, on June 27, I made a statement in the house that persons against whom a prohibitory order had been made would be given an opportunity of making representations to a fact-finding board created for that purpose. Hon. members will notice that this promise has been fulfilled.
Another new feature of the bill is that totally unpaid letters, except of course, those covered by franking privileges, will not be forwarded. The intention of this section is to prevent persons from maliciously sending unpaid letters with the intent of causing annoyance and inconvenience to the addressee.
Franking privileges have been extended in two directions but do not cover special, more costly, services. Under the present law, letters could be forwarded to members of parliament during the ten days before the meeting of parliament free of Canada postage but letters written by members of parliament and sent by them were subject to postage. The new law provides that mail shall be transmitted free during that ten-day period when sent to or by a member of the House of Commons. A new section also grants the same privilege for the ten days following the session, which was not provided for under the old law.
Hon. members will also note that we are recommending the reduction from six to three weeks for the displaying of public notices inviting tenders for mail contracts. The six-week period was stipulated in 1867 and we think that three weeks is adequate under present-day circumstances and faster means of communication. This will speed up the awarding of contracts and establishment of services.
Under the same heading we suggest an increase to $1,000 of the amount under which the Postmaster General may enter into a contract without inviting tenders. The amount suggested is to bring the discretion of the Postmaster General in proportionate line with that which existed in 1867 when the figure of $200 was stipulated. There is no change in principle or practice from that which already exists and the Postmaster General is still under the obligation of not exceeding the amount ordinarily paid for services of a like nature under contracts made after inviting tenders. This proposal will also have the effect of speeding up the awarding of contracts and the establishment of services.

Post Office Act
The same proportional increase is suggested in the awarding of contracts with persons operating a railway, air, steamboat or bus service.
We are also asking the authority in case of emergencies to make whatever arrangements for conveying mail are necessary in the interests of the public service. The washout of the railway lines in British Columbia and the recent railway strike are examples of these possibilities.
I have given the house the highlights of the bill now before it. I shall, when in committee of the whole, give more information about each of these items.
I would suggest for your consideration that details, in regard to operating features, as distinct from items of principle, could more adequately be dealt with when the relevant item is under discussion in the post office estimates, but on the other hand I do not wish in any way to restrict discussion on any related postal problem and shall be glad to deal with any postal matter of importance which hon. members may wish to introduce.
However, I think everyone will agree that it will facilitate the work of the house if we limit as much as possible at this time any discussion on matters of operating detail.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposiiion):
maintopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the
suggestion of the minister that, so far as a discussion of operating details is concerned, in the ordinary course of events it will be better and more convenient to deal with them in committee. However, I do propose to discuss one feature of the bill now before us which goes far beyond any question of operating detail in the effect it will have upon the daily and weekly newspapers of this country.
The minister has reviewed generally the effect of the bill. I think that the amendments which simplify procedure, improve definitions, and provide for the extension of facilities will be welcomed generally by all hon. members. I welcome particularly the provision in the bill to which the minister has referred which makes it possible for him to remedy what I have described as an injustice where there is a different rate within a municipal boundary. I hope that the minister will exercise the power which the amendment proposed would confer upon him in such a way that wherever possible the municipal boundary will be the area within which there will be a uniform rate.
I do not propose to discuss this in any detail at the moment; I simply want to repeat what I have said on earlier occasions and to emphasize the fact that, where there is

a different rate within a municipal boundary, not only is there an injustice upon the person mailing letters or other postal matter, but there is a much greater injustice upon the person receiving this matter because in complete innocence many people direct heavy packages and circulars of all kinds to other people within the municipal boundary thinking that there is a uniform rate, and where such a differential exists penalty postage is imposed on many people simply by virtue of the fact that there is a general assumption that a uniform rate exists within the municipal boundary. I repeat that I welcome this amendment and hope that it will have the widest possible application when it is adopted.
The subject that I wish to discuss in some detail at this time is the increase in the postal rates on daily and weekly newspapers. This is not just a question of dollars and cents; this is not just a question of working out by process of arithmetic what it will cost to handle postal material of this kind. The distribution of news has been recognized for centuries as one of the vital parts of the processes of democracy. The minister pointed out that in recognition of that accepted principle rates have been so arranged for daily and weekly publications ever since confederation that the widest possible distribution of news and cultural information may be available to the people of our country.
We must examine in that light the extent to which the bill now before us proposes to increase postal rates, and consider the effect of the increases in postal rates on daily and weekly publications which are a part of the very living body of democracy in Canada. I think that the rates suggested, when they are carefully examined by hon. members, will be found to be too high as postal rates in the first place in any event, and in the second place they will be found to discriminate against newspapers because magazines and similar publications will pay a great deal less in relation to actual weight and cost of handling.
We have always attached great importance to freedom of the press. May I point out, however, that freedom of the press in itself is relatively ineffective unless there is freedom of distribution and freedom of accessibility which gives to freedom of the press an effective opportunity to leave its imprint upon the minds of the people who determine the course of democracy by the decision and impressions that are very largely formed from this source.
I intend to examine some of the changes that are proposed. I do not intend to discuss the bill section by section because that would not be appropriate on second reading. In order to consider what the effect will be of

adopting the rates proposed, it is however necessary to understand the practical effect of these changes in relation to different types of publications in this country. Canada is in an unusual position. I doubt if the situation in any other nation can be taken as an exact parallel to that which we find in Canada. We are the third largest nation in, the world. The only two nations larger in actual geographical area are Russia and China, one a nation with a population of some 200 million people and the other a nation with a population of close to 450 million.
In our country, only a little smaller than China, we have some 14 million people. Because of that very fact the facilities available for the distribution of news to this widely scattered population become a vitally important part of the whole machinery of democracy which we are doing so much to preserve at this time. While we have large urban communities and many old and well settled smaller communities scattered across this country from the eastern boundaries of Newfoundland to the western boundaries of Vancouver island, nevertheless there are great areas where people are able to have the news in written form only if the facilities are made available on other than a strictly arithmetical postal rate.
In the bill now before us some of the increases are very substantial indeed. In the old act the rates were not only lower but very much lower than those included in the present measure. I would point out that in addition to the burden that will be imposed upon readers through the rates now indicated, there are other burdens which bear directly upon readers of periodicals in Canada. There is a very general tendency to regard taxes of various kinds on corporations as taxes that do not bear directly on the individual Canadian. The sooner we all recognize that taxes imposed upon any business providing a service or a commodity for the public must in the end be paid by the public, the better it will be for our general understanding of the effect of any of these taxes. In Canada it must be remembered that there are already taxes which bear directly on newspapers, and daily newspapers particularly, which are not imposed in the same way upon other types of publications. For instance, there are sales taxes which apply to daily newspapers from which very large publications of much greater weight are exempt. The question may be asked what bearing this has on postal rates. It has a very considerable bearing, because it is part of the general increase in the cost of delivering to individual Canadian
Post Office Act
readers those publications which keep them informed on what is taking place in this country.
The new postal rates will have some very interesting results; and so that we may see exactly what the effect will be let me offer a few illustrations of what these changes will mean in the postal rates on newspapers of different sizes. The new act provides that newspapers and periodicals with a circulation of ten thousand or more copies per issue will pay four cents for each pound weight or fraction thereof. Let us see what will be the actual effect of this on the newspapers of this country. A newspaper of over ten thousand circulation averaging 45 pages for each publishing day now pays $3 a year. Under the new rates it will be called upon to pay $7.64 a year. A newspaper of ten thousand or more circulation with an average of 32 pages for every day of delivery now pays postage of $2.34 a year. The new rate will amount to $6.24. A newspaper of 28 pages in this group which now pays $1.80 postage will pay $4.90 under the new rates. A newspaper of 24 pages which now pays $1.56 in postage will pay $4.19. An 18-page newspaper which now pays $1.36 will pay $3.62. A 14-page newspaper in this group which now pays $1.14 will pay $3.05 if these provisions are adopted.
Then let us take newspapers with a circulation of less than ten thousand. A newspaper with an average of 12 pages and a circulation of less than ten thousand now paying 93 cents will pay $1.54. A newspaper with a 10-page average in this group, which now pays 87 cents, in future will pay $1.31.
Certain changes have been made in regard to newspapers having a limited advertising content. Certain surcharges were imposed upon publications which carried more than 50 per cent of advertising, and that surcharge is done away with. However, there are certain disadvantages as well as advantages in this connection. The fact is that this surcharge did offer encouragement to maintain a certain percentage of news space. The removal of that surcharge also removes that incentive; and regarding this as part of the processes of democracy that should not be considered only as an advantage.
Now I come to the question of the percentage of increase. From the figures I have quoted it will be seen that in many instances the increases are substantially more than 100 per cent. It is very significant that, although such measures have not been adopted, there is a proposal for an increase

Post Office Act
of 60 per cent in the United States. But they are not suggesting that this increase should take place all at once; they are proposing that it be spread over a three-year period, if in fact they adopt the proposal at all. So in a country much more sparsely populated, where the reasons for giving special consideration to those postal services which carry newspapers to the distant parts of the land are much greater than in the United States, it will be seen that we are proposing greater increases than they are even considering over there.
The minister spoke of these special rates as something in the nature of a subsidy. I suggest they have never been regarded as a subsidy, but that they have been regarded and should be regarded simply as part of the whole machinery of democracy, to use the term I have used already. We do not hesitate to spend money on various activities related to the effective working of our democratic system. The various steps carried out under the election act, which in many cases call for the expenditure of substantial amounts of money, would be only partially effective unless the means were provided well in advance of the date of an election for the people to obtain all the essential information they wish to have as to the events taking place from day to day in the local, provincial, national and international fields. I believe the postal rates were mainly regarded as a means by which the rural population of Canada could be supplied with newspapers and periodicals which would give them the essential information they should have. I believe that is the principle which has been accepted in connection with postal rates on matter of this nature.
May I also point out that the newspapers themselves have co-operated in making information available in this way. I believe the record will clearly show that the annual rates at which newspapers are offered to the public give lower returns to the newspapers than any other type of delivery. Just to give one example, an urban daily in any one of the larger cities which sells for five cents a copy, and which in that way would cost $15.25 per year, is generally sold at $10 per year when delivered by post. That, of course, applies to the larger newspapers. In the case of smaller newspapers, there is a lower annual rate charged, although in most cases the street sale is now the same. Thus, it is apparent that the newspapers have been playing their part in making the news available to the widest possible number of readers throughout the whole community.

It is for that reason I believe the minister would be well advised to defer the second reading of this bill, and to review that part of the measure which he is now placing before the house, with the idea that postal rates which will make it easy to continue the widest distribution of daily and weekly newspapers to people in remote parts of this country will be supported by members of this house as part of Canadian democracy itself. I put forward that suggestion in all earnestness. The minister is well aware that there could be little possibility of newspapers absorbing these increased postal rates. It would1 be contrary to the general business practices in any business in this country to expect that very substantial increases of this kind will be carried by the newspapers, although I should think it likely that they will bear some part of the increase.
The bill, as it is before us, would have the effect of discriminating against newspapers at a time when newspapers are more important to the people of this country than they have ever been. No one recognizes more than I do the value of radio, from both the cultural and the news distributing point of view. I certainly welcome the facilities afforded by the radio, as do all hon. members of this house. I am convinced, however, that for the purpose of understanding the issues of the day nothing will ever entirely take the place of the printed word. People's memories may be very good, but it would be very difficult to remember everything that is heard, even in the very best radio programs. I repeat, therefore, that at a time when democracy is threatened, as it has not been threatened for centuries, we should not do anything which will make it more difficult to have the widest possible distribution of the news, or which will be inclined in any way to limit the circulation of those newspapers which have served Canada so well, to the most remote parts of this country from the east to the west, and from the southern boundaries of Canada to its most northerly part.
Some very strong statements have been made about these proposed changes, which indicate the extent of the objection which is being taken- to these proposals. One thing that is emphasized over and over in the statements which have been made already is that it will be the people in the rural districts who will suffer most from a change of this character. It has always been regarded as of the utmost importance that those in the most distant and far-flung points should have these facilities available to them. As was stated in one discussion on this

subject, "This is a direct tax on the intellectual food which is vital to millions of Canadians." I am not suggesting for one moment that at this time the members of this house can disregard the cost of any service that we are called upon to provide through the legislation we adopt. I suggest further that there are ways in which money could be raised from other sources to take care of a substantial part of this deficit to which the minister has referred.
I believe it would be to the benefit of Canadians if comic publications, sex magazines, and crime comics which are still circulated in large quantities were taxed heavily to provide some of the money needed to assist in the distribution to the people of this country of real news about the vital things that are directing the course of affairs in Canada. The strange part about it is that, instead of being taxed, these useless and in some cases dangerous publications actually pay less than those publications which are an essential part of democracy itself. I am not suggesting at all that we should try to decide what the people of this country can read, so long as it is not something that comes within clearly defined criminal or other prohibitions. But I do suggest that the postal service rates and other taxes should be imposed in inverse ratio to the usefulness of the publication. The publications which provide news and cultural information should pay the lowest rates.

I have sought to put forward for the consideration of this house certain reasons why I think that it would be desirable if the minister would withhold this bill from second reading, something which could be done by motion which would, I am sure, be carried by this house if he makes it. If that were done, then before the bill passes to the committee there will have been an opportunity to re-examine those sections which provide these increases in postal rates on the scale that I have mentioned. The minister himself would then not be confronted with the necessity for any hastily-drafted amendments if the arguments which were made by the members in committee convinced him that some changes should be made. If the arguments that I have put forward have merit, I believe that it would assist the minister and the members of this house to have these sections re-examined carefully, without undue haste, so that when the bill has its second reading and goes to committee the minister may have had an opportunity to draft alternative provisions which I think would be consistent with the opinion and with the wishes of many of the hon. members of this house.
At this stage I have sought to avoid some of the exceedingly strong terms which have been employed in editorials and in other public comments on this part of the act. I have refrained from employing some of the strong adjectives that have been employed in responsible newspapers and by responsible men to describe what they think is a serious infringement of democratic rights in this country. I have sought to put forward what I believe would be the wish of the people of Canada, because it will be the people of Canada who will pay the substantial part of any increases of this kind, and it will be they who will suffer if the processes of democracy are weakened in any way at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us is entitled "An act respecting the Canada post office". From what the minister said in his introductory remarks on the motion for second reading of this bill, I assume that it will be in order to discuss some matters pertaining to the post office which are omitted from the bill, as well as those matters which are specifically mentioned. I refer particularly to what the minister termed the operative details of the post office services. While I agree with the Postmaster General that in some respects it would be more convenient to postpone debate on those operative details until the minister's estimates are before the house than it would be to discuss them under this bill, I suggest that there are matters of grave concern to

the Canadian public which, in my opinion, cannot afford to wait until the minister's estimates are before the house.
In a previous speech on this subject in the house I and other hon. members suggested that the time was ripe when either a commission or a special committee of the house should be appointed to investigate the whole question of the post office administration. Under the minister's estimates there will be no opportunity to debate that question in full, and I submit that it is a question that we may well consider while this bill is before us. The leader of the opposition has suggested that second reading of the bill should be deferred. He gave his reasons for asking for that deferment. I would suggest that second reading be deferred in order to consider not only the subject raised by the leader of the apposition but the question of the appointment of a commission or a special committee of the house to investigate the post office administration across this country.
My two chief reasons for suggesting that are that I am constantly, as I am sure all other hon. members are, receiving complaints from citizens that at the present time the post office is not rendering the kind of service for which it has gained a reputation during past years, and the kind of service which the Canadian people expect of the post office. I hear constantly of citizens in areas where there is supposed to be a daily mail delivery having to go for two or three days in succession without delivery of mail; of citizens who are continually obliged to receive their mail delivery after six o'clock at night. I know that I am referring to the Toronto area, and that conditions prevail there which may not prevail in other metropolitan areas. But a very serious situation has developed, and nothing that the Postmaster General or his officials have done within the past month or six weeks in an effort to remedy the situation appears to be very effective.
Only yesterday I met numbers of post office delivery men who still maintain that they are required to work twelve hours a day to cover their routes. That is a condition which, since it still prevails, and since the Post Office Department has already had at least two months or more since the condition was called to their attention to remedy it, and since effective remedies are not being applied, calls for some investigation. I do not think that the government, which in fact should set an example to other employers in this country, should be requiring employees, who by their terms of contract or work are required only to work, or supposed to work, eight hours a day, to work ten and twelve

hours a day without any special remuneration for these extra hours. I am sure we would not condone that practice if engaged in by private employers.
This house would frown upon any employer who engaged men to work for eight hours a day, and then required them to work for ten and twelve hours a day without any remuneration whatever for the extra two, three and four hours a day that they may be called upon to work. These two considerations, the fact that the public in the Toronto area is not now getting the high type of service that is expected of the post office, and that the post office presumes to be giving, and the fact that the delivery men have to work long hours, prompt me to ask that second reading be deferred.
I read in the minister's report that it is the continued effort on the part of the department to cut costs without impairment of service to the public. In the matter of the one delivery a day recently introduced the government has attempted to cut costs. It has also impaired its service to the public by so doing.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this bill which is most important to the people of my constituency. The constituency of Kootenay West, because of its geography, topography and other local circumstances which necessitate some people living in isolated places, is to a great extent dependent upon telephone service. A good and efficient telephone service is most necessary for the district which I have the honour to represent.
Before passing on to my other remarks may I say that we from British Columbia appreciate the interest that some eastern members have taken in this bill. I refer particularly to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) who showed sufficient interest in this bill and the welfare of the people of British Columbia to speak
British Columbia Telephone Company when the bill was last before the house. I want to congratulate the sponsor of the bill upon the presentation-

That Bill No. 116 be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY
speechtext:
That is exactly what I was going to do. I was going to give reasons why I believed this bill should be referred to the committee. Before doing that I want to express my appreciation of the very able way in which the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite), who has no direct interest in this bill because the company does not operate in his constituency, sponsored the bill and presented' the relevant information to the house. I think it only fair to say that, because there have been some occasions on which we have had slipshod presentations of important bills.
We recognize that throughout recent years the British Columbia Telephone Company have carried on extensive expansions in British Columbia and we give them credit for that. But we feel at the same time that we should take advantage of this opportunity to present the requirements of our constituents. Before I give the reasons why I think this amendment should pass may I say that I understand that throughout British Columbia the company has most excellent relations with its employees. I have found that to be generally the case throughout my district. I have found also that in the interior the public relations officials of the company have been most satisfactory. Before proceeding I want first to pay a tribute to the employees of the company in my constituency. Under the most trying conditions during the winter months they have undertaken the most hazardous tasks at times to maintain telephone service to many of our isolated communities.
