British Columbia Telephone Company
It is not my .intention to repeat the arguments so well advanced, toy the hon,. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), but I do want to say that one major reason we consider that this bill should be referred to the committee is that we believe the company is asking for too great an increase in capital at one time. If there was a reduction in the amount of capital asked for it is quite probable that in four or five years they would have to come before this house again and in that way we would -have the opportunity to examine what they had been doing during that period.
Another reason why we think the subject matter of the bill should be referred to the committee is, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned, the very peculiar administrative situation that exists with respect to this company. While the board of transport commissioners has control over tolls, tariffs, and rates, no one has control over services. I understand the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned the fact that the public utilities commission of British Columbia have admitted that they had no power over the services and the development of services of this company.
We believe that there should be an amendment to the act so that some body would have control over services and the development of services according to the requirements of the communities concerned, the same as there is control over power and other utilities. We contend that that would be a very simple matter. Under the health of animals act, the fruit and vegetables act and the forestry act certain provincial officials are empowered to represent the federal government in the administration of certain regulations. We suggest that the act could be amended so that the public utilities commission of British Columbia would represent the board of transport commissioners and be empowered to deal with services and to see that they were properly carried out.
I am going to give other reasons why I think the subject matter of this bill should receive the consideration of the committee according to the amendment. I want to bring to the attention of the house certain complaints that have been brought to my attention with regard to the service given in Kootenay West by the British Columbia Telephone Company. I am going to start with Trail, the silver city of British Columbia, where one of the great metallurgical smelters in the British commonwealth is in operation.
[Mr. Herridge.l

speechtext: They get their silver ore from Kootenay East.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY
speechtext:
I know that, but the manufacturing is done at Trail. That relatively small city makes a great contribution to the industrial welfare and defence production of Canada, yet it is without a modern dial telephone system. For some time they have been asking for an improvement in their telephone services. To illustrate the position briefly, I am going to read an editorial from the Trail Times of March 3, 1951, which reflects public opinion in this matter in that city in my constituency. The heading of the editorial is "Outmoded Telephones". It reads:
The Bell Telephone Company has released some interesting statistics on telephones and one of the most interesting figures, so far as this district is concerned, is that more than 65 per cent of all the world's telephones are dial operated.
The British Columbia Telephone Company, which operates most of the telephone lines in the province, including those in the West Kootenay, makes no distinction in its published reports between dial and other type of instruments but it says there are 4.328 telephones in the Trail area and approximately 230,000 in all of B.C.
Over-all figures on telephone operations show that Canada has an average of one telephone for every five persons. Trail conforms to this average fairly closely. The question of automatic telephones is a far different matter. Trail has no dial telephones. At a time when more than 65 per cent of all telephones in the world have reached the automatic stage it is a sad commentary on a local situation when telephone subscribers here still are plagued with the inconveniences of the "Number, Pulease" system . . . This should not stop Trail from seeking an end to the present central system. After all, so long as there are no protests, the B.C. Telephone Company may imagine Trailites are quite happy with their old-fashioned phones.
I am making a protest in that connection on behalf of the residents of the city of Trail. I want to deal with the golden city of British Columbia, the city of Rossland, which has produced so much gold throughout the years. I wish to read a letter addressed to me by the secretary of the Rossland board of trade, a very responsible organization that considers all things necessary for the advancement of that community. The letter reads:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
Thank you for your letter of February 10 re the British Columbia Telephone Company proposed amending bill.
Of course I had written to And out if they had any complaints.
Also please accept my apology for the delay in replying to same. However, as your letter arrived after our February meeting it was rather hard to get action on it until now. However at last night's meeting the matter was brought up and I can give you the suggestions as handed to me. First of all, I might say that the Rossland board has been dealing with B.C. Telephone company officials during the last year complaining about the service here in

Rossland, and at that time we were given to understand that if this proposed bill went through for authorized capital, the Rossland service would be on the program for an improved system. Naturally then we are in favour of the proposed bill. The suggestions were as follows:
(1)	Installation of a new up-to-date system in Rossland as we have been given to understand that the present party line system is carrying its maximum load and cannot be extended.
(2)	That if improvements are contemplated, consideration be given to the installation of a modern dial phone system.
On behalf of the board I should like to thank you once again for your letter and assure you that you are dealing with a matter which is being followed very closely by this board.
That is the opinion of another considerable section of my constituency. I come to the city of Nelson, the commercial centre of the constituency. There again I have received letters from organizations and individuals complaining of exactly the same conditions complained of by the people of Trail and Rossland. Then I go from there to the capital of the Arrow lakes which the hon. member for Vancouver South knows quite well, the village of Nakusp. It is a small place with a population of some 750 which last year produced 600 carloads of lumber, nearly 550 carloads of cedar poles, and large amounts of farm produce. What do they have to say about it? They are very interested in this telephone bill and in securing improvements in the district surrounding. This is what they ask for, and they have been asking for these things for some time. That is one reason, Mr. Speaker, why we believe the amount of capital being asked for is too large. We believe these companies should have to come to the house fairly frequently for their increases in capital so that members of the house will have an opportunity to give expression to the complaints of their constituents. This letter is from the secretary of the Nakusp board of trade, and reads:
In reply to your letter re the B.C. Telephone Company which came to hand last week, would advise you that at our regular meeting held on Tuesday 20th, I was asked to give you the following points for consideration in the matter:
1.	Twenty-four hour service.
We have not got twenty-four hour service. The operator has to be wakened at night if someone is sick and we wish to telephone Nelson, Trail or some other outside point. The letter continues:
2.	Individual lines in town, or at least for business premises.
3.	Fewer phones on existing party lines.
These are matters which we have been tackling for some time but we just get promises and no action. Hoping something can be done in this direction in the near future,
Yours truly,
Thos. Mitchell
British Columbia Telephone Company
There is another reason why we wish to see the money that will be raised as a result of this bill spent to a somewhat greater extent in the interior of British Columbia. I come now to Slocan which is producing a large amount of galena, lead, zinc, silver and metals of that type. I have heard from their board of trade, and they have been trying for years to get some improvements in that mountainous area where telephone service is very necessary, particularly when the roads between Sandon and New Denver, and other points, are blocked by slides in winter and when the only communication is by telephone. This is what I am advised by the secretary of the Slocan district board of trade with its headquarters in New Denver, a very lovely village, the Switzerland of North America. The letter reads:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
Re: B.C. Telephone Company
Thank you for your letter of February 10, and I trust that this reply is not too late to reach you before the proposed amending bill comes up for discussing in the house. We have been in correspondence recently with the B.C. Telephone Company requesting a regular twenty-four hour service in the New Denver exchange, but as yet have received no satisfactory reply. There is also a pressing need for more lines to Silverton, the present thirty-six phones in that thriving base metal mining community being served by only six multi-party lines. The number of telephones in Slocan city should also be increased, but we are not prepared at this time to recommend what form the improvement to service in that centre should take.
This district has received excellent service and co-operation from the company's district agent at New Denver, in spite of the fact that her work has been made most difficult due to the overcrowding of lines, shortage of adequate help due to the fact that the present emergency service set-up precludes a regular shift schedule being followed, etc. As a matter of fact, this lady is now under medical care at the coast following a nervous breakdown. We certainly hope that something can be done to bring the telephone service here into line with present-day business demands, as we feel that this is one part of the province where the increase in demand for telephones approximates the increase in capitalization being requested by the telephone company.
That letter is signed by Mr. N. F. Brookes, secretary of the Slocan district board of trade. Then I come to a somewhat unusual situation with respect to the Salmo and district valley where we have several large gold producers and several other mines including the Emerald mine, which will shortly be producing tungsten for the defence effort, and a large mine which is now being developed by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, the Hudson Bay mine. For some years they have been trying to get improvements in service in that small community where there is an immense production of wealth, and so far they have not received the attention from the company that they

British Columbia Telephone Company deserve. In that connection I want to read a letter from their secretary. It is as follows:
I wish to acknowledge receipt of your letter of February 10-
You will note that I wrote them all on the same day.
-concerning the above, for which we thank you. Please be advised that this board is not at all satisfied with the telephone service now being provided in the Salmo area. At present the B.C. Telephone Company provides line service to the exchange in the Salmo post office and to the F. R. Rotter Lumber Company, but does not operate a service in the area itself. This service is managed on an individual proprietor basis by Mr. L. H. Lund, the present postmaster. This board has set up a special committee to go into the whole problem of improving the telephone service in the area. On numerous occasions in the past, the officials of the B.C. Telephone Company at Nelson have been contacted with a view to interesting them in providing a service for this area. The present holder of the phone franchise, Mr. Lund, has invited the company to make him an offer for his exchange, lines and equipment. This the company has refused to do, explaining that the equipment is valueless to them and that therefore they cannot reasonably pay him anything for it.
This board takes the position that, as a public utility, the B.C. Telephone Company has an obligation to provide an improved phone service in this area, regardless of whether or not they can expect a profit from operations in the region. Their profits from operations in larger centres would assuredly take care of any operating deficit in this area.
Anything you could do to convince the company that they should make an effort to provide a sorely needed improved service in this area, would be greatly appreciated. It seems that, in order to set up such an improved service, the company would have to buy out the service rendered by Mr. L. H. Lund, and then set up either an exchange or a dial system, such as is being installed in Castlegar and Fruitvale. We feel that the expansion going on in this area justifies consideration of such a step by the company in any event.
We would appreciate any information you can give us on the above problem.
Yours very truly,
(sgd.) F. T. Middleton,
Secretary
This community still suffers from a poor telephone service.
I am not going to read any more letters, because others will want to say a few words on this bill. These illustrations, I think, indicate the need for some authority within the province to exercise control over the service rendered by this company to the people of British Columbia, particularly in the rural areas. The same thing applies to Kaslo, a small incorporated city in my district, from which I have had communications along exactly the same lines. They are not satisfied with their telephone service. Only recently in that city there have been great developments in connection with the utilization of carbon dioxide for dry ice. Already a large sum has been spent, and they expect within two or three years to have a million dollar

plant in that little city. The same thing applies at Castlegar, at the end of the Arrow lakes, and at Robson and other Arrow lake points. The same thing applies at Fruitvale, a growing community which is trying hard to get improved telephone service. There is need for improvement and expansion all through the district, and the people I represent have been doing their best to get that improvement and expansion. This is the only opportunity I have to bring their needs to the attention of the house.
Before concluding I should like to deal with another peculiar situation; that is the matter of telephone service in the Lardeau valley. At one time the Canadian Pacific Railway operated a railway line between Lardeau and Gerrard, a distance of about 32 miles. In 1941 they abandoned that line, turning the roadbed over to the provincial government for a highway, and also turning the telegraph wires over to the provincial government for the use of the forest service. Since then the whole line has deteriorated and been allowed to fall into disrepair. Here we have an area with 500 million feet of virgin standing timber within an area of a few square miles, as well as large mineral deposits and 16,000 acres of the best land in British Columbia awaiting settlement. Various residents of that area, as well as the board of trade, wrote to ask if I would bring the matter to the attention of the federal government to see if they would do something to assist them in maintaining this telephone service. The minister informed me the matter would be investigated. It has been investigated, and I am advised that the cost would be too great to be considered at the present time but that the Department of Transport will give technical advice to the settlers of the area if they wish to maintain the line at their own expense.
My point is that this service should be undertaken by the British Columbia Telephone Company. Why should they be allowed to have the profits from the rich districts like Vancouver, New Westminster, Victoria, Burnaby and so on, the cream of the telephone crop, and refuse to give service to other areas? subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock for dinner I was in the process of explaining why I thought the Post Office Department needed a thorough housecleaning job done. I shall conclude these remarks with one more reference. I think, Mr. Speaker, it might be an appropriate time to consider whether or not it would be advisable to have the administration of the post office removed from the jurisdiction of a department of government, such as is at present the case, and have the administration placed under a commission similar to that which now operates our Canadian government railways. I am quite confident that such an arrangement would offer fewer opportunities for the practice of political patronage in connection with the Post Office Department than exist at the present time.
To my own personal knowledge it is just about impossible today for anyone who is not a well-known supporter of the Liberal party to get permission even to operate a sub-post office in some little cubby hole of a back shop or store in our cities and suburban municipalities. There are many opportunities for the distribution of political patronage in the post office system outside the civil service

and from all I can gather the present administration takes full advantage of those opportunities.
I want to turn now to the matter raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), the change in rates for the carriage of newspapers and periodicals. The minister told us last year that his department lost approximately $12 million on the handling of newspapers and periodicals. The department is asking us to condone a reorganization of the department in connection with mail deliveries, a reduction in the public service, for the express purpose of saving something like $3 million. It is not reasonable that we should condone an economy of that nature and at the same time condone a loss of $12 million by one branch of the postal service. I am not familiar with these rates but I presume that the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) and his officials have estimated the new rates so that they will just about cover the cost of these services. There is more information we need but it probably will be forthcoming in committee.
I should like to know whether periodicals published and printed outside Canada and distributed in Canada will be subject to the same rates as periodicals published in Canada. I should like to know if the recent increase in the postal rate on unsealed drop letters containing mimeographed and printed notices from one cent to two cents, an increase of 100 per cent, is based on the cost of the service. I should like to know if the Post Office Department was losing half what it cost to provide that particular service; that the service cost the department just twice as much as it was receiving.
I contend that the various branches of the Post Office Department should pay their own way. In this connection I should like to call attention to an article which appeared in Maclean's Magazine of August 15,	1949, just after the federal
election.
This article refers to two Toronto dailies which, by the way, are the largest English language evening papers published in Canada. Both these papers profess allegiance to democratic ideals and have declared that it is the duty of a newspaper to give impartial information on all sides of any question that is of public interest. As a matter of fact, the heads of both newspapers are on record to that effect in the editorial columns of their papers. Here is how impartial these papers were during the last election campaign. During the last week of the campaign the Toronto Daily Star gave five times as much news space to the Liberal party at it did to the Progressive Conservative party. The Toronto Telegram gave five times as much space to the Progressive Conservative party as it did to the Liberal. Both are supposed to be independent in politics. I would say that both, like many other newspapers in Canada, at election time at least degenerate into party propaganda sheets. The Star gave the C.C.F. party 2.4 per cent of its political news coverage in that week, and the Telegram gave the C.C.F. 2.6 per cent. There is not much choice between them.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I welcome this opportunity to consider this bill, which is designed to bring post office legislation up to date. It has been our belief for quite some time that an opportunity should be provided to thoroughly consider all matters relating to general post office policy. we urge that this course of action be followed. Our feeling is that this bill should be referred to a committee of this house.
My understanding of what the minister said this afternoon is that this bill has two specific purposes, first to bring post office legislation up to date and second to eliminate redundant sections of the old act. We have no argument to offer with respect to those two purposes. Certainly it is time the act was brought up to date, and certainly these redundant sections should not longer remain in the legislation. I agree with the minister that such matters as actual operating details should be considered when the post office estimates are before the house, and that we should relate our discussion specifically to policy when considering this bill.
I do not intend to occupy the time of the house now by referring to any specific sections of the bill, which I assume would be out of order; but I would like to serve notice upon the minister that I for one intend to question him in quite some detail on a number of very important aspects of policy. One has to do with the appointment of postmasters. My conviction is that the present method is entirely wrong. When we come to the relevant section I propose to elaborate upon that assertion, and may refer to certain specific cases to indicate why I feel the policy is wrong. Moreover, I think the time has arrived when we should give serious consideration to the conditions under which certain postal employees work, their hours of work, conditions of work and salaries.
Perhaps at this point I should say that during the years I have been privileged to serve as a member of the House of Commons my relationship with local postmasters, with district office officials and with head office officials has been most cordial. I have frequently commented upon the excellence of the work done by these various groups of post office employees. I have often wondered, however, how many of them chafe from time to time under certain restrictions and conditions under which they work. How they must chafe when trying to carry out certain aspects of post office policy which I think, if the truth were known, they believe should have been changed long since.
Another matter I intend to pursue at some length in the discussion of the bill is the service given in certain communities. I want to say a word with respect to this bill, which is of great interest to the people of this country. I have had quite a lot to do with the institution of rural routes but very little to do with the appointment of postmasters, except in minor offices. I have been in politics for a long time, and the only postmasters I have tried to replace as such were those who had taken the positions of Liberal postmasters when Mr. Bennett was elected to office. I have left them alone except when there were complaints from interested parties, customers of the post office, for technical reasons. I did not even visit them. I believe I am one of the few members of parliament who have not visited each post office in their counties. My impression is that when we hear no complaints about a post office it means it is well run; that has been my experience. So long as I had no complaints I did not want to interfere with the management of the post office. But at times there were complaints. I remember Mr. Veniot, who was one of the greatest postmasters general whom I have known, and the next best is the present incumbent. In the meantime, there were postmasters general of various abilities. Some were very hard to deal with, and others' paid very little attention to the duties inherent in their position. Some others organized a system of secrecy concerning the reports coming to the department, and which are not supposed to be known to members of parliament.

Post Office Act
If there is a request made for any change or any improvement in the Post Office Department, a member of parliament should be entitled to know what report was made by the local inspector; what report was made to Ottawa by the district inspector; what recommendation was made by the head of the branch to the deputy minister; and what recommendation was made by the deputy minister to the minister. I have admiration and affection for the present Postmaster General, and he may rely on my support because he deserves it. I say the same of his parliamentary assistant. But so long as I support the minister and his parliamentary assistant, it does not mean that I have to swallow all the high officials we have in the Post Office Department in Ottawa. Some of them have been there for a long time, and some not so long.
My idea of a good civil servant is one who respects his minister, and who shows loyalty to the head of the department; not only that, but one who understands that for the good management of any department there shall be respect for the hierarchy within the department. The deputy minister is not the head of the department. He is the deputy head, and he should behave accordingly. The man who has the responsibility for the management of the department is no one else than the head of the department-this applies to all departments. Since I was first elected I have known very few postmasters general who have been just as assiduous in their parliamentary as in their departmental work, but that is the case with the present Postmaster General of Canada. The tribute that I pay him tonight is a well deserved tribute, because I have a profound respect for anyone who works with so much intelligence.
I wonder if I should recall what I said one day in a caucus in the province of Quebec. I said that the present Postmaster General is an intelligent man. There was loud applause. Then I said, "Your applause, gentlemen, is no compliment to his illustrious predecessor, but I will not insist." Sir, the members of parliament are supposed to be the collaborators of the cabinet ministers, especially of the Postmaster General. I do not see much partisan politics in any department; but since the time I had the postmasters and mail carriers reappointed who had suffered great injustice from the Bennett regime, I have not recommended anyone merely because he was one of my supporters. I have enough respect for the intelligence of the people in my constituency not to recommend any one of my supporters

who was not perfectly qualified to occupy a position in the Post Office Department or elsewhere.
Members of parliament, sir, make recommendations for the appointment of postmasters to minor post offices. For post offices having a gross revenue of $3,000, the appointment is made on the recommendation of a member of parliament, and above that it is by the civil service commission. Well now, what I have tried to do was to make the civil service commission understand the danger of appointing one who was not fully qualified to serve the community as it deserves to be served. Until now we have been quite successful, and in my constituency the Post Office Department has been abiding by the provisions of the Post Office Act, and the Civil Service Act concerning military preference.
Every time that a returned man was asking-for a vacant post office, so long as he was qualified he was recommended. But what happened was that after their appointment some resigned. They said they would not keep the job. Then the department had the trouble of appointing other men who sometimes also resigned. Those arfe difficult matters, especially with regard to men suffering from disabilities. The matter should be looked into with a view to making the least possible number of appointments within a certain period of time and seeing to it that in the first place men who will be the most useful are selected.
I give credit to the minister for his co-operation. I also give credit to most of the officials of his department, especially those outside Ottawa. I do not complain of all of the personnel of the post office department in Ottawa but I remember well that among the high officials there is one whom I could not thank at any time because I had some trouble with him. The only way to fix it up was not to deal with him at all. He was vicious; he still is. I hope he will soon go. This is one example.
Others try to create trouble for members of parliament, in the name of efficiency, with the pretext of streamlining the department on all sides. Others play at intrigue by coaxing some members of the press gallery, apparently giving them false scoops. They are hard to deal with. But to establish and to maintain order in any department is not fascism; it is order. The idea of order has been so much lost sight of in the minds of the people that whenever anyone tries to establish it he is accused of interfering with the efficiency of a smooth-working system.

You know well, Mr. Speaker, what is the basis of good government. It is plain common sense, fair play and respect for sound, established practices.
There is something else to which I wish to refer. There is to be taken care of not only the distribution of mail in the Post Office Department but also the delivery of mail to all the recipients of it throughout the country. The Post Office Department is a big one with a revenue of, I would imagine, about $100 million a year and with a large number of employees. I pay tribute to the personnel of the Post Office Department, as I said, with the exception of a few plants that have grown too high. In the spring it is time to cut the weeds. But the average personnel is good and has a good spirit. That is something which has been inspired by the minister himself, by the parliamentary assistant and by those employees of the Post Office Department who have been trained in the right manner by those who have a high sense of duty and who have more public spirit than private selfishness and ambition.
To come back to the mail routes and to the delivery of mail, as hon. members know the delivery is made in cities by letter carriers who are appointed by the civil service commission outside of the jurisdiction-and most of the time outside of the knowledge-of members of parliament. The staff of the city post offices is also appointed by the civil service commission. I have not much more to say, but with regard to rural routes there is one thing that should be considered, namely the differences of level, the differences in the kinds of roads on which the mail carrier will have to go in order to deliver the mail, the hills, and so on. It is impossible to have a flat average of $50 per mile. There may be some cases where it is a reasonable payment for the services of the mail carrier, but in others it is not. If a man has to climb hills for the delivery of mail, he evidently deserves more than the one who travels on a flat route. This is one point which should be left to the good judgment and the fairness of the minister, at least in appeal from the decision previously rendered by those in charge.
I am glad that, in virtue of the new act which is before the house now, the minister will have authority to make his own decisions up to $1,000, I believe. Is that it?

speechtext: What about the weeklies?

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I am not forgetting the weeklies because if there is any press that is more or less non-political, if there is any press that is non-partisan, if there is any branch of the press in Canada which helps to form an important part of this great fourth estate of this great dominion, it is the weekly press. I pay my tribute to the weekly press of Canada. I hold no brief, and as I grow older I hold less brief, for those who disagree with the party I support. I know there are some that do not support the Conservative party very solidly; there are others that support it rather clumsily; but we do have freedom of the press, of the fourth estate as it is called, that means so much to the life of the country.
Our press means much in the education of this country. Not all hon. members within sound of my voice, let alone many men in the far-flung areas, are able to send their boys and girls to universities. There are many families that cannot afford to do that. There are many families that have to work hard; there are many great minds in Canada who have learned to toil with their -hands but who have learned from the daily press. I pay that tribute to the press of Canada. Thank God we have a free press in Canada. They have done more generally and broadly for the education of our people, for the inspiration to try to do better in the future, for the

inspiration of trade and industry, for the inspiration to develop charitable and social services, for the inspiration to develop and increase social services and church work, than they are given credit for.
We find now that the government seeks to impose a penalty which in normal times or in times of the slightest depression would be a crushing blow to many small weeklies. There is not one within sound of my voice who does not know of many weeklies throughout the country that have been selling annual subscriptions for $2 and still having difficulty in getting enough subscribers to make their advertising rates profitable. In 1930 the tax per ton on newsprint used for the dissemination of news in this dominion was fifty cents, and today the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) proposes that it shall be $10.20. The Canadian producers of newsprint receive less for the newsprint they deliver to Canadian publishers, but the Canadian publishers pay substantially more than the United States publishers. The United States publishers pay $106 per ton, but with these taxes as they stand now the Canadian publisher will pay $111.20 per ton, when all these taxes are included. There is a ten per cent sales tax on the daily and weekly papers, yet the crime and sex comics and all these nonsensical s^ets which add nothing to the culture of this dominion pay no sales tax.
Let us be fair. I agree with the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that the Postmaster General is genial and always looks like a fair fellow. In so far as I am concerned I think he has been fair. I urge him to take this back to cabinet council and review this act. I know that no government of Canada could impose this tax at the present time without realizing that there are bound to be many repercussions. I know we have the bureau of publicity here in Ottawa which is growing like a mushroom. We have the C.B.C. and the other means of disseminating news for the government. In fact, the government is becoming the greatest publisher in Canada. Now we have the government curtailing others.
We have the publications sent out by the Department of Agriculture. I know the Minister of Agriculture authorizes all this and I try to read it, but my wastepaper basket is full of the things I receive from that department which I have not time to read. The Department of Trade and Commerce do likewise. Being somewhat interested in the newsprint industry I would say that if it were not in short supply I might almost welcome the waste of newsprint there is by the dominion government.
Post Office Act
It does surprise me that now they are curtailing its use by the imposition of this tax. They are going to impose a tax of approximately $3 on many of the rural newspapers in Canada, or double their present rates. I ask hon. members to pause and realize what it will mean to those in the far-flung areas, the miners, the people in the bush and others in isolated sections who have hesitated to send in subscriptions at $2.50 if they are now asked to pay $5.50?
This seems to be in keeping with the trend of a government that has been in power too long. This is a trend toward the curtailment of the press. It is a trend that has been indicated all along the line in the curtailment of the press in different ways, to submerge the news instead of disseminating it. There are many services that are necessary in this great country, vast as it is, sparsely settled as it is. This fact has been recognized since the days of confederation. The transportation of our vast resources, the transportation of our people in the far-flung areas, has been paid for more or less by the state. Immigration which is needed to improve and increase our population is paid for by the state. The dissemination of news for the education of our people should also be considered part of our nation building.
This seems to me to be a grave error on the part of the government. At least it is an oversight. I would be unfair if I said that it was intentional, but whether it is intentional or an oversight it will discourage the dissemination of news. It will weaken the prestige of the fourth estate in this dominion. It will curtail the freedom of the press. It will create hardship for many who feel it is a hardship to pay the present annual subscriptions but who still want to know what goes on outside their local districts. It will create a hardship for those whose only means of learning is the daily and weekly press.
I urge the government to reconsider its move in this regard and try to get the revenue somewhere else. You have the comic strips, you have the sex magazines, you have the crime sheets and other sources of revenue.

They may be a .little to the left, they may be too far to the right, but in many cases they are not permitted to print news outside of what is of local interest.
No matter what the issue is, no matter what policy is being followed, the people should know what is going on. This tax imposing a restriction on the dissemination of news is more dangerous to our democratic way of life in these modern times than at any other time in our history. There has never been a time in our history when people have craved knowledge more than they do now. There has never been a time when the dissemination of news has been more vital to our very existence. If the freedom of the press never dies in Canada, communism will never live in Canada.

I agree with you perfectly, Mr. Speaker.
I was about to say that if press reports are correct concerning the deputy postmaster general, to the effect that he is trying to stamp out patronage in the post office, he has my wholehearted support; and I am glad to know that he is listening to that comment at this moment.
However, I really rose to speak on one matter of principle that is covered by the bill now before us. I shall reserve any more extended remarks about it until we get to the section of the bill dealing with the letting of contracts, but since this is the time we discuss the general principles involved I felt I would like to say a few words about this matter now.
I refer to the practice of letting out under contract the collection of mail from post office letter boxes scattered around our cities. I should not speak for all cities in Canada, but I do know the situation in my own city of Winnipeg and I have reason to believe it is similar if not identical to that in other cities. In Winnipeg we have these trucks painted red with the words "Canada Post G.R." on the side, which travel about the city picking up letters and parcels from the street letter boxes. Similar trucks deliver mail from the post office to the trains, to airports and so on. I have no doubt most people in my city assume that those trucks and various delivery vehicles are owned by the Post Office Department and that the men who drive them and do this work are employees of that department. In the city of Winnipeg that is not the case. This work is let out by contract; as a matter of fact there are a number of contractors depending on the particular service in question. This in turn means that the drivers of these trucks, sometimes referred to as mail couriers, are not civil servants and employees of the Post Office Department, but are employees of the contractors to whom this_work has been let.
My plea to the Postmaster General and his department is that consideration be given to placing that work directly under the aegis

Post Office Act
of the department. I make that plea particularly in the name of the employees concerned. In my view the mail couriers in Winnipeg are not getting a proper break in the matter of wages, hours, holidays, pension rights, sick leave and all the other working conditions, comparable to what is enjoyed by civil servants. When from time to time some of us take up the plight of these people with the department we are simply told that the Post Office Department is not the employer of these men, that they are employed by the contractors to whom this work has been let, and that they must apply to their immediate employers for any improvement in working conditions. I find further that there are different types of contracts, and that these contracts have varied over the years. Some have escalator clauses; others have not. Sometimes when a group of employees appeals to the contractor for an improvement in wages or working conditions, the employer appeals to the government for an increase in the amount paid under the contract. Sometimes the government answers that plea, an increase is given and the improvement takes place. On other occasions the contractor does not pass on the plea, or if he does the government does not see fit to increase the amount paid. As a result there are variations between one type of service and another, as well as between cities, in the wages and working conditions of these men.
My study of this whole matter, arising out of close contact with the men involved, leads me to assert that the whole situation is quite unsatisfactory. The men can go on pursuing the present practice of trying to get their employers to improve their conditions, which sometimes results in their employers trying to get better contracts. But there is always a lag as far as the men are concerned, and they are woefully behind the conditions enjoyed by other civil servants and people doing comparable work in a place like my own city.
That is the case. I shall deal with it in more detail when we reach that section of the bill; in fact when that time comes I shall present facts and figures as to wages, hours of work, lack of pension privileges and matters of that kind. I did feel, however, that at this stage when we are discussing the principle of this new legislation, I should bring to the attention of those who deal with these matters the urgent need of reviewing this whole situation as far as mail couriers are concerned and with respect to these trucks that they drive about the city picking up the mail.

Before doing so, however, I should like to follow up the excellent observations made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) in connection with this indirect tax upon the dissemination of news in Canada.
These days we read of the suppression of newspapers like La Prensa in Buenos Aires; we read of the request by French journalists and newspapers for the allocation of additional newsprint to help promote, establish and maintain the principles of our free way of life, and it seems to me that we in parliament have an obligation, as the minister and the government have a very special duty, to see to it that while we are attempting to establish those principles in the broad international field we do not do something to undermine the very same principles at home by means of domestic legislation such as this. It may be argued, as it has been argued in this debate, that the tax is not ruinous, that it will not be felt so heavily. In my view, however, the imposition of additional financial obligations upon those disseminating news in Canada is a retrograde step for which I do not think the government can take much credit at this time. I should like the minister to consider the possibility, even at this time, of leaving things as they are at least for the time being, while this nation and others who feel as we do are engaged in a strenuous struggle for survival and for the continuance of our free way of life.
I do not want to indulge in unnecessary forensics in connection with a matter of this kind, but I think it goes to the very root of our democratic system. While we have free postage on Hansard containing our speeches in this house; while we have the free distribution of all the propaganda, if you like, coming from government departments in the form of news, statements of policy and the like-and I have not heard of any tax going on that-in the final analysis I wonder-

Along with our parliamentary system, they form our democratic system. You cannot separate the two. One is complementary to the other. When you attempt, even, by this method which is employed here, to impose a burden upon the dissemination of that news, you not only attack the press itself but indirectly you are attacking parliament. I cannot, therefore, be too emphatic in expressing to the minister my belief that he should review that part of this post office bill.
If I may, I should like to come to another point which has not been dealt with in this debate, and that is why we have to keep on forgetting the forgotten man. This has been going on now not for years but for decades. There never seems to be enough influence brought upon the minister or upon the government with respect to the plight of the rural mail couriers to have the government act in any definite way. Here we have a great shake-up-at least, I suggest one may call it a shake-up-in our Post Office Department and a number of amendments made to that act. There has been some talk about overhauling an act which has been there since 1867. If we are going to overhaul the act, then why do we not overhaul some of the regulations that need overhauling the most? Here we are taxing newspapers and the dissemination of news, and at the same time doing nothing for the rural mail couriers across this country. While perhaps for some urban people the rural mail courier just appears to be another contractor, that is not the case. Those of us who have been served by rural mail during the many years of our farm life realize that the rural mail courier is much more than just a contractor. Post Office Act
they regard as a proper solution of this difficult problem. After the rural mail couriers have come to Ottawa and given their complaints to a committee, then I would be satisfied with whatever decision was made. I want to emphasize to the minister that I think we at least owe that much to them.
In view of the fact that this is an opportunity for dealing with the Postmaster General's department in general, there is another point I wish to bring to his attention. In places like the constituency I represent, which has been growing perhaps more rapidly than most sections of Canada and in which there are literally hundreds of houses going up year after year with new areas opening up, it seems to me that the question of extending the rural mail or postal delivery service to meet that condition is essential and urgent today. I know that the department is making some effort to meet the situation as they find it. If a committee is formed-I hope the minister has not entirely closed the door on that-that is one question I should like brought before the committee. In the United States there has been adopted some scheme whereby these suburban communities are being serviced by a sort of in-between system, that is between the postal delivery service and the regular rural mail delivery. I should like to see the committee deal with that question as well.
So I say to the minister that when the act is being overhauled, these matters ought to be considered. Once the act is finally passed with such amendments as may be necessary during its tour through the legislative chamber, we may not have an opportunity of satisfying the rural mail couriers that their case has not been glossed over by any procedure of parliament which does not give them an opportunity of being heard.
I am not asking for impossible reforms. All I am asking for is to have them heard. If it is then determined that the present system of contract is the best, I think the minister will have satisfied the couriers, the public and parliament. More than that, he will have done something which is perhaps more difficult: he will have satisfied me.

It has been said that these new rates are taxes. May I say that they are not taxes.	They are fees for services

rendered. Up till now we have been rendering these services for $15 million and have been collecting only about $3,900,000. With the proposed increase, we shall add another $2 million only on the services rendered the newspapers. That will amount to about $6 million that we shall collect from the newspapers and magazines, out of an expenditure of some $16 million this year and probably much more next year on account of the increase in the cost of transportation, wages, et cetera. *
It has been suggested that the second reading of this bill should be deferred until time has been given to review this section. If the house would like to have the assurance that the section itself might be deferred for further consideration, I have no hesitation in giving it in order to weigh all the arguments that have been made here. I might say, however, that consideration has already been given to practically all of these suggestions. I must point out to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that deferring the second reading of the bill would of itself prevent the establishment of certain postal areas in which he might be interested.
The increases that we have made here are not confined to Canada. Similar increases have been made in the United States. It has been suggested that the increase in the United States is only 60 per cent and spread over three years. That is correct. But one must remember that in the United States the deficit in the postal department for the last operation year was $599 million. I should not like to see my department facing a somewhat proportionate deficit.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to answer all the questions at this time. I will come to them in committee. There is one thing, however, that I must answer, namely the question of charging more to certain types of newspapers. Reference has been made to comic magazines. The comic strips included in the papers of course are carried at the same rate as the newspapers. When we come to the comic magazines my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, has not been well informed, because comics do not enjoy the privilege that he has quoted. Comics have to pay on the regular circular rate of two cents for one ounce or a fraction thereof, and one cent for each ounce over that. Therefore the comic magazines or the sex magazines that have been mentioned pay nine cents a pound as compared with the four cents that we are charging for the big newspapers.
I might point out here-it might be of some interest-that if we had collected the amount

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will move to go into supply and ask for interim supply. We will not call any new departments. I understand that this is a formality. Then we will revert to the study of the post office bill.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, May 30, 1951
